Here 'description' includes a thing's essential qualities, not just those added to it. A definition may identify the whole nature, part of it, or something outside it. Likewise, a feature that cannot be separated from a thing may be essential or incidental. Although we can describe things through their outward parts, philosophers more often define them through the parts distinguished by the intellect.

The mention of organs and shapes recalls the author's difficulty about understanding a whole person intellectually. We must not remove something essential and then pretend we still understand the complete person—as the saying asks, who has ever seen a lion without tail, head, or belly?

The intellectual human being therefore has sight and eyes, but at its higher level these mean its direct knowledge of what lies beneath it, including things that are seen. It has hearing and ears in the same sense, as direct knowledge of sounds, and similarly for imagination and other powers. Its hand is its effective power to act.

At the level where it is expressed in bodily forms, its sight and eyes appear through the many particular acts of seeing and the many eyes that perform them. The same is true of its other organs and powers. We must, however, understand these bodily powers as dependent on the intellectual reality and connected to it, not as detached pieces accidentally placed beside it.
The presence of incidental features does not prevent a universal from being understood. They can also be left out when needed.

The world of direct creation and the world in which things are brought forth are not far from you, though you see them as distant. You are nothing other than these worlds; nothing else will remain of you or be enough for you—especially the higher world of intellect, in which the knower and what is known are one. If you doubt what we have set before you, consider the reality of what is understood: the vastness of that existence, its unity despite containing many things, its light, and the way it illuminates things outside the mind. Do not stop at the meanings of things as mere concepts.

This is why I have said that the teaching that one simple reality contains all existences in a higher and simpler way is, in truth, a teaching about knowledge. To perceive something is to find and reach it; the meeting of luminous existence with luminous realities is itself knowledge. Bodily meeting is only so called by analogy, since bodies touch one another only at their edges and surfaces. That is why the mystics call the higher realm the world beyond separation. Perception through the body is not true perception in the way intellectual understanding is.
How could an image be lost and then restored if the Active Intellect were not always present? The state of one thing united with another follows the state of the other.

As when the soul's understanding of the Light of Lights, unity, simplicity, or all-encompassing existence remains as a faint image. It can then retrieve the intelligibles from its simple intellectual state and picture them in imagination and sensation.
If “particulars” means immaterial particulars, then direct recognition is a higher level than ordinary knowledge.
One may support this view with the saying, “The first duty in religion is to know God; the perfection of knowing is to affirm Him,” which treats knowing and assent as distinct.
It is easy to affirm that the things we sense exist.
The point is not that recognition means conception. Rather, we must first affirm that a thing exists before asking what its essence is.
More precisely, it is not the thing itself that is preserved, but its trace. The text may be read: “the thing disappeared and its trace remained.”

Some claim that spirits began later but preceded bodies by two thousand years, citing a report that spirits were created two thousand years before bodies. They connect this to the primordial covenant. The author notes that this view still leaves unexplained what caused each individual spirit to begin.

On this view, the spirits did not exist as separate individual essences; they existed through God and His detailed knowledge. Their acknowledgment praised God's greatness, dominion, and glory. Forgetting Him means becoming absorbed in nature and its scattered, dark forms.

They have not understood the point of the Qur'anic words, “He sends down water from the sky, and valleys flow according to their capacity.” The gifts received depend on the capacities of the matter and natures that receive them. Nor have they understood “The likeness of His light is as a niche in which there is a lamp.” His light is the intellect fully active within the intellect that has acquired the ability to understand, which in turn is within the intellect still capable of learning; or it is the universal intellect in the universal soul, which is in universal nature. The same pattern continues through the other levels.

Earlier in this stage, “intellect” had other meanings. In Keys to the Unseen, it is also defined as the soul's natural ability to reach certainty about universal, true, necessary premises without proof or deliberate thought. This differs from the intellect in potential; it is a strong readiness for acquiring such knowledge.
This refers to the word “good”; the definition also explicitly mentions action.
The phrase describes doing work well, which is not itself wisdom. Wisdom is the knowledge that guides the work.
Do not assume from “mental existence” that the mind itself has a mental existence. The phrase means existence that is related to the mind.
The mind is the soul's readiness to acquire beliefs and opinions it does not yet have.
More exactly, knowledge is the beginning and end of worship, and worship follows from it.
The discussion of this point has already appeared earlier.

Knowledge has been defined as belief that excludes the opposite; opinion as belief that favors one side without excluding its opposite; and certainty as belief that something is so, together with belief that it cannot be otherwise. Earlier logicians were right to say that only certainty is knowledge in the strict sense. If the opposite remains possible, the belief is not necessary; and if the favored conclusion itself remains possible rather than necessary, it is not certain. Later logicians were mistaken to divide knowledge into certainty, compound ignorance, and other kinds.
